program_plain: World: a ring road of 1000 cells with 300 cars, each with a speed from 0 to 5. Rules each step, all cars at once: (1) speed up by 1 if below 5; (2) slow to the number of empty cells ahead if that is smaller; (3) with probability 0.3 slow down by 1; (4) move forward by the speed.
model_family: Probabilistic cellular automaton / statistical physics of traffic (particle-hopping models, ASEP extensions)
standard_name: Nagel-Schreckenberg model: spontaneous (phantom) jams and stop-and-go waves
citations: Nagel & Schreckenberg 1992, J. Physique I 2:2221-2229 - original NaSch CA; transition from laminar flow to start-stop waves with increasing density
Chowdhury, Santen & Schadschneider 2000, Physics Reports 329:199-329 - standard review of particle-hopping traffic models incl. NaSch
Maerivoet & De Moor 2005, arXiv physics/0509082 'Cellular Automata Models of Road Traffic' - second review (reference list only seen)
Nagel & Paczuski 1995, Phys. Rev. E 51:2909 'Emergent traffic jams' - jam dynamics (seen only as a reference-list entry)
Barlovic et al. 1998, Eur. Phys. J. B 5:793 - VDR model; NaSch shows stop-and-go but no phase separation (via secondary source)
searches: Nagel Schreckenberg cellular automaton model for freeway traffic 1992 spontaneous jams
review Nagel-Schreckenberg model stop-and-go waves Chowdhury Santen Schadschneider statistical physics of vehicular traffic
notes: Rules map exactly onto NaSch with vmax=5, p=0.3, density 0.3 (ring L=1000, N=300). The 200-car and p=0.1 variants are lower-density / lower-noise NaSch parameter regimes with weaker jamming (thresholds not checked in a source). Full text of the 1992 paper and the Physics Reports review were not read; claims rest on abstracts and citing papers. Burstiness (activity CV) and spectral-peak readouts were not directly found in a source; they are my inference from jam birth, decay and recurrence.
full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The rule system is the Nagel–Schreckenberg (NaSch) traffic cellular automaton, and the behaviour you observed is its standard, textbook behaviour.

**1. Model family.** This is a probabilistic cellular automaton from the statistical physics of traffic, in the class of particle-hopping models and the asymmetric exclusion process with extensions. Your four rules are the NaSch rules: accelerate, brake to the gap, random slowdown, then move. The parameters are vmax=5, p=0.3, and density 0.3 (300 cars on 1000 cells). One source describes NaSch as an elaboration of rule 184 with a variable discrete velocity, acceleration, deceleration due to other vehicles, and a random tendency to slow down.

**2. The behaviour.** At this density and noise level the system is in the congested regime, where spontaneous "phantom" jams form without any bottleneck. These jams are the localised stop-and-go clusters you measured. They match your readouts as follows:
- **Many separate domains and spatial clustering (g_n_domains, g_moran):** jams appear as separate clusters of slow or stopped cars.
- **Bursty activity (g_activity_cv):** the jam clusters grow and dissolve, so local activity fluctuates strongly.
- **Dominant temporal frequency (g_spec_peak):** the backward-moving jams recur at a roughly regular rate, which gives a spectral peak.

I did not find a source that explicitly describes the burstiness or the spectral peak. The jam clusters themselves are well documented. The spectral peak is my inference from the recurring jams, not something a source confirmed.

**Earliest clear source.** Nagel & Schreckenberg, "A cellular automaton model for freeway traffic", J. Physique I 2, 2221–2229 (1992). Its abstract says Monte-Carlo simulations show a transition from laminar traffic flow to start-stop waves with increasing vehicle density. The reference list in arXiv cond-mat/0410074 confirms the citation details: Kai Nagel and Michael Schreckenberg, A cellular automaton model for freeway traffic, Journal de Physique I France, 2:2221–2229, 1992.

**Review.** Chowdhury, Santen & Schadschneider, "Statistical physics of vehicular traffic and some related systems", Physics Reports 329, 199–329 (2000). A search result gives this as Phys. Rep. 329, 199–329 (2000). That review is the standard reference for the NaSch model.

**Related sources:**
- Maerivoet & De Moor, "Cellular Automata Models of Road Traffic" (arXiv physics/0509082), is a second review. I confirmed only its reference list, not its text.
- Nagel & Paczuski, "Emergent traffic jams", Phys. Rev. E 51, 2909 (1995). The search returned it only as an entry in a reference list. It is the dedicated study of jam dynamics.
- Nagel, "Life-times of simulated traffic jams", Int. J. Mod. Phys. C 5, 567 (1994), also appeared only as a reference-list entry (in arXiv cond-mat/0410074).
- One source says the NaSch model shows stop-and-go waves, but no phase separation. Phase separation appears only with a slow-to-start rule, as in the VDR model (Barlović et al. 1998). Your model has no slow-to-start rule, so jams are transient clusters, not one large phase-separated jam. That fits your "many domains" reading.

**Parameter variants.** 200 cars is a density of 0.2, and p=0.1 is lower noise. In NaSch both still give jams, but they are weaker, rarer and shorter-lived. At low density or low noise the system can stay in free flow. I did not verify the exact thresholds in a source. They don't change the verdict, since this is the same model family in a different parameter regime.

**3. Confidence: high** that this is the NaSch model and that spontaneous jams and stop-and-go waves are its known behaviour. I confirmed the 1992 paper and the review through their citation details. I could not read the full text of the 1992 paper or the review, so my statements about their contents rest on abstracts and citing papers. Confidence is lower for the burstiness and spectral-peak readouts specifically, since no source I found describes them.
